current_answer: The strongest early U.S. warning is hiring: a Census working paper finds that 22- to 24-year-olds in the most AI-exposed industry-state cells were hired less often after ChatGPT's launch. That is a serious signal, not a settled AI job-loss count. The study uses exposure rather than observed adoption and finds pandemic-era, remote-work and education trends tangled with the same industries. In Denmark, linked records show task reorganization but no detectable earnings or recorded-hours effect in the first two years. AI is changing work faster than the broad outcome data can yet prove a single story.

catalogue_card.question: Are entry-level jobs already being hit by AI?
catalogue_card.text: A U.S. working paper finds a sharp early-career hiring drop in the most AI-exposed industries. The warning is real; its cause is not settled.

summary: U.S. administrative-data research finds a persistent relative drop in hiring of 22- to 24-year-olds in the most AI-exposed industry-state cells after ChatGPT's launch. The author identifies plausible non-AI explanations that still need to be separated.

A Census firm survey finds AI use is substantial in employment-weighted terms, while most AI-using firms report task augmentation only. Firm-reported AI-related employment declines were rare in that survey window.
A Danish linked-data study rules out earnings or recorded-hours effects above 2% over its first two years, while finding new AI-related tasks and occupational movement among adopters.
Global exposure is broad but is not a layoff count: the ILO estimates that one in four workers are in occupations with some generative-AI exposure.
uncertainty: No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.
The U.S. early-career result is an exposure-based association, not a clean firm-adoption experiment.
Hiring, employment, wages, hours and task content can move differently across countries and occupations.
